info.name: LogEngin — ITSM Multi-Agent Platform
info.description:
Full API surface for the ITSM multi-agent support platform (FastAPI + LangGraph). Generated from the actual route decorators and Pydantic request models in src/api/routes/*.py and src/api/main.py by scripts/generate_postman_collection.py — every request body here matches a real schema, not a guess.

**Setup**
1. Import this collection AND the companion environment file.
2. Select "LogEngin Local" in Postman’s environment picker (top-right).
3. Run **Auth > POST /login** once if you need a real user session (most endpoints work unauthenticated in dev mode via X-Tenant-ID alone — see src/api/deps.py get_auth_context).
4. Run **Tickets, Approvals & MCP > POST /api/v1/tickets** to populate {{thread_id}}/{{ticket_id}} for the requests that depend on them.

See docs/deployment.md and docs/live-environment-readiness.md for what's real vs. mocked in this environment.

request.description:
Read a ticket by the ``sr-tkt-…`` reference shown next to a session.

Producers record that reference, not the internal ``thread_id``, so without
this the console had to download a page of tickets and search it in the
browser — capped at 50, which made every older reference look missing.

Prefers the full thread serialisation so a ticket renders identically
however it was reached. That view needs live workflow state (or a stored
demo detail) though, and neither survives a restart — so a ticket still
listed in the console would answer 404 here, which is the same "it's right
there but I can't open it" problem in a new place. When the richer view
isn't available, the registry's own record is returned instead: fewer
fields, but true ones.
Return the ordered, client-readable profiles for all agent tiers.

Check whether a proposed skill is compatible with the target agent tier.

Reports, from both perspectives:
  * input gap  — required inputs the agent cannot currently supply
  * output gap — platform-required outputs the skill does not declare
plus a tier-fit recommendation and duplicate detection.
Latest SR01 business-health snapshot + trend summary (no ticket needed).
Manually trigger an SR01 continuous health sweep (operator-forced).
Pending/decided SR01 ticket candidates for the operator approval queue.

Approve a pending candidate — creates the real ticket via the normal
Master → L1 pipeline and records the ticket reference.
Reject a pending candidate; its fingerprint keeps deduping in-window.
Latest SR02 detection snapshot + trend summary (no ticket needed).
Manually trigger an SR02 detection sweep (operator-forced).
Pending/decided SR02 ticket candidates for the operator approval queue.

Approve a pending candidate — creates the real ticket via the normal
Master → L1 pipeline and records the ticket reference.
Reject a pending candidate; its fingerprint keeps deduping in-window.
Start a new SR03 interactive chat session.
Send a user message to SR03 and return the bot's TurnResult.

Submit the one-time code on a separate route so it never sits in chat
history (the engine redacts any code-looking input before persisting).

DEV/DEMO ONLY — reveal the one-time code the MockNotifier "sent" so an
operator can complete the verify step during a live demo.

The real code is deliberately NEVER logged and NEVER written to the
transcript (Phase-2 security; the ``sr03_no_secret_in_transcript`` and
``test_otp_code_never_appears_in_logs`` guards enforce that).

**The gate is the notifier, not the LLM.** This only ever reads the
in-process ``MockNotifier`` outbox — i.e. a code that a *fake* sender
produced and delivered nowhere. The moment a real notifier (SES/SMS) is
wired in, this returns 404, so a genuinely-delivered code can never be
revealed. (Gating on ``mock_llm`` would be wrong: the notifier is mock in
this POC regardless of whether the LLM is real.) The chat UI shows its hint
only when this endpoint answers.
One session plus its (secret-free) transcript.

Remove one session and its transcript.

Deliberately a stronger permission than reading the results table beside it:
this destroys a record, and ``metrics:read`` is granted for looking.

Any ticket the session raised is **left alone**. A ticket is a commitment to
a person that outlives the conversation that created it, and deleting a
tidy-up row in a demo list must never quietly close real work. The session's
identity-audit rows survive for the same reason.
Recent chat sessions for the tenant, optionally filtered by status.
Settings + honest self-service metrics for the SR03 card (Phase 6).
Update app_config["sr03"] (shallow merge onto existing overrides).

Start enrolling an authenticator app. Returns the seed **once**.

The response is secret-bearing, so it is never logged and never audited; the
audit row is written at *confirmation*, which is the moment the factor
actually becomes usable.

Prove the authenticator really holds the seed. Until this succeeds the
enrolment authorises nothing.

Who is in the demo directory and which of them are locked.

Without this you have to guess: an unlock walkthrough against an account
that happens to be unlocked reports "not locked" and the story dies, and
there was no way to see that ahead of time.

Set a demo account's lock state, so a walkthrough can be run again.

An unlock demo needs something locked, and the first successful run removes
exactly that. Without a way back you get one rehearsal and then a flow that
reports "was not locked" forever. ``locked=false`` puts an account the other
way, for rehearsing the "nothing to unlock, shall I reset instead?" branch.

The account is created if it is not there, so a name can be introduced and
used immediately — the same freedom ``SR03_DEMO_ACCOUNTS`` gives at startup.

Remove an enrolled factor. Idempotent and non-enumerating: revoking one
that never existed reports the same success, revealing nothing.

Whether this user has a *confirmed*, unrevoked factor.

Carries no secret material of any kind — no seed, no otpauth URI, no counter.
``confirmed_at`` is included because the enrolment panel displays it; it is a
timestamp, not a credential.

Chatbox "test this agent" action on the sub-agent profile page: build a
real ticket from pasted log/incident text and dispatch it straight to this
sub-agent's owning tier (bypassing Master's routing so the target agent is
guaranteed to run), then return that agent's result for display.
Analyze infrastructure logs and continue workflow (create ticket + route by log signals).
Poll raw log stream entries (unclassified until error/alert detected).
Start unified raw log stream; each line is typed, alerts are queued and processed sequentially.

request.description: Run log analysis + infrastructure impact and persist to DB.
Create ticket and run master agent only; persist results to DB.

Serve the reset form.

Always 200 with the same page, valid token or not: deciding validity here
would tell an attacker which tokens are live before they ever post one.

Serve the unlock page.

Always the same 200 whatever the token, for the reason the reset page does
it: deciding validity here would tell an attacker which links are live
before they ever post one.

Redeem an unlock link and end the lockout.

Reached only after the same CAPTCHA the reset page uses, which is why the
check for it comes first: holding the link lets you *ask*, passing the check
is what acts.

Two properties worth stating, because they are what make "check your email"
honest. The account is untouched until this call, so an unopened link leaves
the lockout exactly as it was. And the link is spent only once the directory
has actually unlocked — a provider error leaves it usable rather than
burning the requester's one chance.

Issue a fresh CAPTCHA for the reset page.

Deliberately takes no token and reveals nothing: it is drawn before we know
whether the link is any good, so requesting one cannot be used to find out.

The answer is signed into ``challenge`` rather than stored, so this endpoint
holds no state, needs no cleanup, and works across workers and restarts.

Check the CAPTCHA and, if it passes, open the password step for this link.

**Be clear about what this establishes.** It establishes that a human is on
the page. It does *not* establish which human — so from here, whoever holds
the emailed link can set the password. That is a deliberate product choice
replacing the authenticator challenge that used to sit here; the security
consequence is written down in ``docs/SR03-MFA-DEMO-GUIDE.md`` rather than
left for someone to discover.

What still protects the link: it is 32 random bytes, single-use, expires in
30 minutes, and every attempt here is rate-limited per IP and audited.
Redeem a token and apply a password the user chose themselves.
